title: Faithful John
description: A servant saves his king three times at the cost of turning to stone.
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once upon a time an old king who was ill, and thought to himself: 'I am lying on what must be my death-bed.' Then said he: 'Tell Faithful John to come to me.' Faithful John was his favourite servant, and was so called, because he had for his whole life been so true to him. When therefore he came beside the bed, the King said to him: 'Most faithful John, I feel my end approaching, and have no anxiety except about my son. He is still of tender age, and cannot always have good counsel. If you do not promise me to teach him everything that he ought to know, and to be his foster-father, I cannot close my eyes in peace.' Then answered Faithful John: 'I will not forsake him, and will serve him with fidelity, even if it should cost me my life.' On this, the old King said: 'Now I die in comfort and peace.' Then he added: 'After my death, thou shalt show him the whole castle: all the rooms and apartments, and all the treasures and everything the castle contains; but thou shalt not show him the last chamber in the long gallery, in which is hidden the portrait of the Princess of the Golden Dwelling. If he sees that portrait, he will fall violently in love with her, and will drop down in a swoon, and will undergo great danger for her sake, therefore thou must preserve him from that.' And when Faithful John had once more given his promise to the old King about this, the King said no more, but laid his head on his pillow, and died. When the old King had been carried to his grave, Faithful John told the young King all that he had promised his father on his death-bed, and said: 'This I will assuredly keep, and will be faithful to thee as I have been faithful to him, even if it should cost me my life.' When the mourning was over, Faithful John said to him: 'It is now time that thou shouldst see thine inheritance. I will show thee thy father's palace.' Then he took him about everywhere, up and down, and let him see all the riches, and the magnificent apartments, only the one room where the dangerous portrait was, was not opened. The portrait, however, was so placed that when the door was opened you looked straight on it, and it was so splendidly painted that it seemed to breathe and live, and there was nothing more charming or more beautiful in the whole world. The young King, however, observed that Faithful John always walked past this one door, and said: 'Why dost thou never open this one for me?' 'There is something within it,' he replied, 'which would terrify thee.' But the King answered: 'If I have seen all the palace, I want to know what is in this room also,' and he went and tried to force the door open. Then Faithful John held him back and said: 'I promised thy father before his death that thou shouldst not see what is in this chamber; it might bring the greatest misfortune on thee and on me.' 'Oh, no,' replied the young King, 'if I do not go in, it will be my certain destruction. I should have no rest day or night till I had seen it with my own eyes. I shall not leave the place now until thou hast unlocked the door.' Then Faithful John saw that there was no help for it now, and with a heavy heart and many sighs, sought out the key from the great bunch. And when he had opened the door of the room, he entered first, and thought by standing before him he could hide the portrait so that the King should not see it in front of him, but what was the good? The King stood on tiptoe and saw it over his shoulder. And when he saw the portrait of the maiden, which was so magnificent and shone with gold and precious stones, he fell fainting to the ground. Faithful John lifted him up, carried him to his bed, and sorrowfully thought: 'The misfortune has happened, Lord, what will become of us?' Then he strengthened the King with wine, until he came to himself again. The first words he spoke were: 'Who is that beautiful maiden?' 'That is the Princess of the Golden Dwelling,' answered Faithful John. Then the King continued: 'My love for her is so great, that if all the leaves on all the trees were tongues, they could not declare it. I will give my life to win her. Thou art my most faithful John, thou must help me.' The faithful servant considered for a long time how to set about the matter, for it was difficult even to get into the presence of the Princess. At length he thought of a way, and said to the King: 'Everything which she has about her is of gold: tables, chairs, dishes, goblets, bowls, and household furniture. Among thy treasures are five tons of gold; let one of the goldsmiths of the kingdom work these up into all manner of vessels and utensils, into all kinds of birds, and wild beasts and wonderful animals, such as will please her, and we will go there with them and try our luck.' The King ordered all the goldsmiths to be brought, and they had to work night and day until at last the most splendid things were prepared. When everything had been laden on board a ship, Faithful John put on the clothes of a merchant, and the King was forced to do the same, in order to make himself quite unrecognizable. Then they sailed across the sea, and sailed on until they came to the town wherein dwelt the Princess of the Golden Dwelling. Faithful John bade the King stay behind on the ship, and wait for him. 'Perhaps,' said he, 'I shall bring the Princess with me, therefore see that everything is in order; have the golden vessels set out and the whole ship decorated.' Then he gathered together in his apron all kinds of gold things, went on shore and walked straight to the royal palace. When he entered the courtyard of the palace, a beautiful girl was standing there by the well with two golden buckets in her hand, drawing water with them. And when she wanted to carry away the glittering water she turned herself round, and saw the stranger, and asked him who he was. Then he answered: 'I am a merchant,' and opened his apron, and let her look in. Then she cried out: 'Oh, what beautiful gold things!' and put her pails down and looked at one after the other. Then said the girl: 'The Princess must see these, she has such great pleasure in golden things, that she will buy them all from you.' She took him by the hand and led him upstairs, for she was the waiting-maid. When the Princess saw the wares, she was quite delighted and said: 'They are so beautifully made, that I will buy them all of thee.' But Faithful John said: 'I am only the servant of a rich merchant. The things I have here in my apron are not all, and my master has in his ship the finest and greatest of them.' She wanted to have everything brought to her, but he said: 'There are so many of them that it would take a great many days to bring them, and so much space would be required to exhibit them, that your house is not big enough.' Then her curiosity and longing were still more excited, until at last she said: 'Take me to the ship, I will go there myself, and behold the treasures of thy master.' Then Faithful John was quite delighted, and led her to the ship, and the King, when he beheld her, saw that her beauty was even greater than the picture had represented, and thought nothing else but that his heart would burst in twain. Then she climbed on board the ship, and the King led her within. Faithful John, however, remained behind with the pilot, and ordered the ship to be pushed off, saying: 'Set all sail, till it flies like a bird in air.' Within, however, the King showed her the golden vessels, every one of them, the dishes, goblets, bowls, and the birds and wild beasts, and the wonderful animals. Many hours went by whilst she was seeing everything, and in her delight she did not observe that the ship was sailing away. After she had looked at the last, she thanked the merchant and wanted to go home, but when she came to the side of the ship, she saw that it was on the deep sea far from land, and hurrying on with all sail. 'Ah!' cried she in her alarm, 'I am betrayed! I am carried away and have fallen into the power of a merchant — I would rather die!' The King, however, seized her hand, and said: 'I am not a merchant. I am a king, and of no worse birth than thou art, and it is my love for thee which has caused me to carry thee away. The first time that I saw thy portrait, I fell fainting to the ground.' When the Princess of the Golden Dwelling heard this, she was comforted, and her heart was inclined unto him, so that she willingly consented to be his wife. It happened, however, while they were sailing onwards over the deep sea, that Faithful John, who was sitting on the fore part of the vessel, making music, saw three ravens in the air, which came flying towards him. Whereupon he stopped playing and listened to what they were saying to each other, for he knew their language well. One cried: 'Oh, there he is carrying home the Princess of the Golden Dwelling.' 'Yes,' replied the second, 'but he has not got her yet.' Said the third: 'But he has got her, she is sitting beside him in the ship.' Then the first began again, and cried: 'What good will that do him? When they come on land, a fox-red horse will spring towards them. Then he will want to mount it, and if he does, it will leap away with him into the air, so that he will never see his bride again.' Said the second: 'Is there no escape?' 'Oh, yes, if any one else gets on it swiftly, and takes out the pistol which must be in its holster, and shoots the horse dead with it, the young King is saved. But who knows that? And whosoever knows it, and tells it, will be turned to stone from the toe to the knee.' Then said the second: 'I know more than that; even if the horse be killed, the young King will still not keep his bride. When they go into the palace together, a wrought bridal garment will lie there in a dish, and seem to be woven of gold and silver, but it is nothing but sulphur and pitch, and if he puts it on, it will burn him to the very bone and marrow.' Said the third: 'Is there no escape?' 'Oh, yes,' replied the second, 'if any one with gloves seizes the garment and throws it into the fire and burns it, the young King is saved. But what avails that? Whosoever knows it and tells it, half his body will become stone from the knee to the heart.' Then said the third: 'I know still more; even if the bridal garment be burnt, the young King will still not keep his bride. When the dance is over, and the bride is gone to sleep, the Queen will come and take the young Queen's necklace from her neck, and throw it into the sea, and then the young Queen will die.' Said the second: 'Is there no escape?' 'Oh, yes,' said the third, 'if any one takes the necklace from the sea and gives it back to the young Queen, the young King is saved. But whosoever knows it, and tells it, will be turned to stone from head to foot.' When the ravens had thus spoken, they flew onwards, and Faithful John had well understood everything, but from that time forth he became quiet and sad, for if he concealed what he had heard from his master, the latter would be unfortunate, and if he revealed it to him, he himself would have to die. At length, however, he said to himself: 'I will save my master, even if it bring destruction on me.' When therefore they came on shore, all happened as had been foretold by the ravens, and a magnificent fox-red horse sprang up. 'Well,' said the King, 'he shall carry me to my palace,' and was about to mount, but Faithful John got before him, jumped quickly on it, drew the pistol out of the holster, and shot the horse. Then the other servants of the King, who after all did not wish well to Faithful John, cried out: 'How shameful to kill the beautiful animal, that was to carry the King to his palace!' But the King said: 'Hold your peace and let him alone, he is my most faithful John, who knows what good this may be for?' They went into the palace, and in the hall there stood a dish, and therein lay the bridal garment, looking as if it were woven of gold and silver. The young King went towards it and was about to take hold of it, but Faithful John pushed him away, seized it with gloves, carried it quickly to the fire, and burnt it. The other servants again began to murmur, and said: 'Look, now he is even burning the King's bridal garment!' But the young King said: 'Who knows what good he may have done, let him alone, he is my most faithful John.' Now the wedding was celebrated: the dance began, and the bride also took part in it; then Faithful John was watchful and looked into her face, and when she went into her chamber he followed her, and when the Queen came and took the necklace from the young Queen's neck and threw it into the sea, Faithful John, who had been watching, sprang down into the sea and fetched it out, and brought it back to the young Queen. The young King was overjoyed when he saw his bride again, and knew not how to thank his faithful servant enough. But Faithful John, who had saved his master three times, now grew silent and sad, and the King asked: 'Faithful John, why are you so sad?' He answered: 'I have done my duty, and now I must die.' Then the King was terrified, and said: 'I will do all in my power to save you.' But Faithful John told him everything that the ravens had said, and how he must turn to stone. The King wept, and said: 'Oh, my most faithful John, I will pray day and night that thou mayest not be turned to stone.' But already Faithful John's feet were turning to stone, then his knees, then his body to his heart, and at last his head, and he stood there as a stone statue. The King and Queen were in great grief, and the King said: 'Ah, how ill have I rewarded such great fidelity!' And he had the stone statue placed in his bedchamber beside his bed. As often as he looked at it, he wept and said: 'Ah, if I could bring thee back to life, my most faithful John!' Some years passed, and the Queen bore two sons. One day, when the King was looking at the statue and weeping, he heard a voice which said: 'If thou wilt cut off the heads of thy two children with thine own hand, and smear the statue with their blood, Faithful John will come back to life.' The King was horrified, but he thought of Faithful John's great fidelity, and how he had died for him, and he drew his sword, and with his own hand cut off the heads of his children, and smeared the statue with their blood, and Faithful John came back to life, and stood before him hale and strong. Then said he to the King: 'Thy faithfulness shall not go unrewarded,' and in the same moment the children came running in, and were merry and glad as if nothing had happened. Then the King was full of joy, and the Queen too, and they lived happily together ever after.

Faithful John, however, remained behind with the pilot, and ordered the ship to be pushed off, saying: 'Set all sail, till it flies like a bird in air.' Within, however, the King showed her the golden vessels, every one of them, the dishes, goblets, bowls, and the birds and wild beasts, and the wonderful animals. Many hours went by whilst she was seeing everything, and in her delight she did not observe that the ship was sailing away. After she had looked at the last, she thanked the merchant and wanted to go home, but when she came to the side of the ship, she saw that it was on the deep sea far from land, and hurrying on with all sail. When the Princess of the Golden Dwelling heard this, she was comforted, and her heart was inclined unto him, so that she willingly consented to be his wife. It happened, however, while they were sailing onwards over the deep sea, that Faithful John, who was sitting on the fore part of the vessel, making music, saw three ravens in the air, which came flying towards him. 'Yes,' replied the second, 'but he has not got her yet.' Said the third: 'But he has got her, she is sitting beside him in the ship.' Then the first began again, and cried: 'What good will that do him? When they come on land, a fox-red horse will spring towards them. And whosoever knows it, and tells it, will be turned to stone from the toe to the knee.' Then said the second: 'I know more than that; even if the horse be killed, the young King will still not keep his bride. When they go into the palace together, a wrought bridal garment will lie there in a dish, and seem to be woven of gold and silver, but it is nothing but sulphur and pitch, and if he puts it on, it will burn him to the very bone and marrow.' Said the third: 'Is there no escape?' 'Oh, yes,' replied the second, 'if any one with gloves seizes the garment and throws it into the fire and burns it, the young King is saved. But what avails that? Whosoever knows it and tells it, half his body will become stone from the knee to the heart.' Then said the third: 'I know still more; even if the bridal garment be burnt, the young King will still not keep his bride. When the dance is over, and the bride is gone to sleep, the Queen will come and take the young Queen's necklace from her neck, and throw it into the sea, and then the young Queen will die.' Said the second: 'Is there no escape?' 'Oh, yes,' said the third, 'if any one takes the necklace from the sea and gives it back to the young Queen, the young King is saved. But whosoever knows it, and tells it, will be turned to stone from head to foot.' When the ravens had thus spoken, they flew onwards, and Faithful John had well understood everything, but from that time forth he became quiet and sad, for if he concealed what he had heard from his master, the latter would be unfortunate, and if he revealed it to him, he himself would have to die. At length, however, he said to himself: 'I will save my master, even if it bring destruction on me.' When therefore they came on shore, all happened as had been foretold by the ravens, and a magnificent fox-red horse sprang up. 'Well,' said the King, 'he shall carry me to my palace,' and was about to mount, but Faithful John got before him, jumped quickly on it, drew the pistol out of the holster, and shot the horse. Then the other servants of the King, who after all did not wish well to Faithful John, cried out: 'How shameful to kill the beautiful animal, that was to carry the King to his palace!' But the King said: 'Hold your peace and let him alone, he is my most faithful John, who knows what good this may be for?' They went into the palace, and in the hall there stood a dish, and therein lay the bridal garment, looking as if it were woven of gold and silver. The young King went towards it and was about to take hold of it, but Faithful John pushed him away, seized it with gloves, carried it quickly to the fire, and burnt it. The other servants again began to murmur, and said: 'Look, now he is even burning the King's bridal garment!' But the young King said: 'Who knows what good he may have done, let him alone, he is my most faithful John.' Now the wedding was celebrated: the dance began, and the bride also took part in it; then Faithful John was watchful and looked into her face, and when she went into her chamber he followed her, and when the Queen came and took the necklace from the young Queen's neck and threw it into the sea, Faithful John, who had been watching, sprang down into the sea and fetched it out, and brought it back to the young Queen. The young King was overjoyed when he saw his bride again, and knew not how to thank his faithful servant enough. But Faithful John, who had saved his master three times, now grew silent and sad, and the King asked: 'Faithful John, why are you so sad?' He answered: 'I have done my duty, and now I must die.' Then the King was terrified, and said: 'I will do all in my power to save you.' But Faithful John told him everything that the ravens had said, and how he must turn to stone. The King wept, and said: 'Oh, my most faithful John, I will pray day and night that thou mayest not be turned to stone.' But already Faithful John's feet were turning to stone, then his knees, then his body to his heart, and at last his head, and he stood there as a stone statue. The King and Queen were in great grief, and the King said: 'Ah, how ill have I rewarded such great fidelity!' And he had the stone statue placed in his bedchamber beside his bed. As often as he looked at it, he wept and said: 'Ah, if I could bring thee back to life, my most faithful John!' Some years passed, and the Queen bore two sons. One day, when the King was looking at the statue and weeping, he heard a voice which said: 'If thou wilt cut off the heads of thy two children with thine own hand, and smear the statue with their blood, Faithful John will come back to life.' The King was horrified, but he thought of Faithful John's great fidelity, and how he had died for him, and he drew his sword, and with his own hand cut off the heads of his children, and smeared the statue with their blood, and Faithful John came back to life, and stood before him hale and strong. Then said he to the King: 'Thy faithfulness shall not go unrewarded,' and in the same moment the children came running in, and were merry and glad as if nothing had happened. Then the King was full of joy, and the Queen too, and they lived happily together ever after.

description: A boastful tailor becomes king by wit, giants, unicorn and all.

chapters.text: One summer's morning a little tailor was sitting on his table by the window; he was in good spirits, and sewed with all his might. Then came a peasant woman down the street crying: 'Good jams, cheap! Good jams, cheap!' This rang sweetly in the tailor's ears; he stretched his delicate head out of the window, and called: 'Come up here, dear woman; here you will get rid of your goods.' The woman came up the three steps to the tailor with her heavy basket, and he made her unpack all the pots for him. He inspected all of them, lifted them up, put his nose to them, and at length said: 'The jam seems to me to be good, so weigh me out four ounces, dear woman, and if it is a quarter of a pound that is of no consequence.' The woman who had hoped to find a good sale, gave him what he desired, but went away quite angry and grumbling. 'Now, God bless this jam for me,' cried the little tailor, 'and give me health and strength'; so he brought the bread out of the cupboard, cut himself a piece right across the loaf, and spread the jam over it. 'That won't taste bitter,' said he, 'but I will first finish the jacket before I take a bite.' He laid the bread by him, sewed on, and in his joy, made bigger and bigger stitches. In the meantime the smell of the sweet jam ascended to the wall, where the flies were sitting in great numbers, so that they were attracted and flew down on it in hosts. 'Hola! who invited you?' said the little tailor, and drove the unbidden guests away. The flies, however, who understood no German, would not be turned away, but came back again in ever-increasing companies. The tailor at last lost all patience, and drew a piece of cloth from the hole under his work-table, and saying: 'Wait, and I will give it to you,' struck it mercilessly on them. When he drew it away and counted, there lay before him no fewer than seven, dead and with legs stretched out. 'Art thou such a fellow?' said he, and could not help admiring his own bravery. 'The whole town shall know of this!' And the little tailor hastened to cut himself a girdle, stitched it, and embroidered on it in large letters: 'Seven at one stroke!' 'What, the town!' he continued, 'the whole world shall hear of it!' and his heart wagged with joy like a lamb's tail. The tailor put on the girdle, and resolved to go forth into the world, because he thought his workshop was too small for his valour. Before he went away, he sought about in the house to see if there was anything which he could take with him; however, he found nothing but an old cheese, and that he put in his pocket. In front of the door he observed a bird which had caught itself in the thicket. It had to go into the pocket with the cheese. Then he took the road boldly, and as he was light and nimble he did not feel tired. The road led him up a mountain, and when he had reached the highest point of it, there sat a powerful giant looking about him quite at his ease. The little tailor went bravely up, spoke to him, and said: 'Good day, comrade, so thou art sitting there overlooking the wide-spread world! I am just on my way thither, and want to try my luck. Hast thou any inclination to go with me?' The giant looked contemptuously at the tailor, and said: 'Thou ragamuffin! Thou miserable creature!' 'Oh, indeed?' answered the little tailor, and unbuttoned his coat, and showed the giant the girdle. 'There mayest thou read what kind of a man I am!' The giant read: 'Seven at one stroke,' and thought that they had been men whom the tailor had killed, and began to feel a little respect for the tiny fellow. Nevertheless, he wished to try him first, and took a stone in his hand and squeezed it together so that water dropped out of it. 'Do that likewise,' said the giant, 'if thou hast strength.' 'Is that all?' said the tailor, 'it is child's play with us!' and put his hand into the pocket, brought out the soft cheese, and pressed it until the liquid ran out of it. 'Faith,' said he, 'that was a little better, wasn't it?' The giant did not know what to say, and could not believe it of the little man. Then the giant picked up a stone and threw it so high that the eye could scarcely follow it. 'Now, little mite of a man, do that likewise.' 'Well thrown,' said the tailor; 'but after all the stone came down to earth again; I will throw you one which shall never come back at all,' and he put his hand into his pocket, took out the bird, and threw it into the air. The bird, delighted with its liberty, rose, flew away and did not come back. 'How does that shot please you, comrade?' asked the tailor. 'You can throw well,' said the giant, 'but now we will see if thou art able to carry something proper.' He took the little tailor to a mighty oak tree which lay there felled on the ground, and said: 'If thou art strong enough, help me to carry the tree out of the forest.' 'Readily,' answered the little man; 'take thou the trunk on thy shoulders, and I will raise the branches and twigs; after all, they are the heaviest.' The giant took the trunk on his shoulder, but the tailor seated himself on a branch, and the giant who could not look round, had to carry away the whole tree, and the little tailor into the bargain: he behind, was quite merry and happy, and whistled the song: 'There were three tailors riding forth,' as if carrying the tree were child's play. The giant, after dragging the heavy load part of the way, could go no further, and cried: 'Hark you, I shall have to let the tree fall!' The tailor sprang nimbly down, seized the tree with both arms as if he had been carrying it, and said to the giant: 'Thou art such a great fellow, and yet canst not even carry the tree!' They went on together, and as they passed a cherry-tree, the giant seized the top of the tree where the ripest fruit was hanging, bent it down, gave it into the tailor's hand, and bade him eat. But the little tailor was much too weak to hold the tree, and when the giant let it go, the tree sprang back again, and the tailor was hurried into the air with it. When he had fallen down again without injury, the giant said: 'What is this? Hast thou not strength enough to hold the weak cherry-tree?' 'There is no lack of strength,' answered the tailor. 'Dost thou think that could be anything to a man who has struck down seven at one blow? I leapt over the tree because the huntsmen are shooting down there in the thicket. Jump after me, if thou canst.' The giant tried it, but could not get over the tree, and remained hanging in the branches, so that in this also the tailor kept the upper hand. The tailor looked round and thought: 'It is much more spacious here than in my workshop.' The giant showed him a bed, and said he was to lie down in it and sleep. The bed, however, was too big for the little tailor; he did not lie down in it, but crept into a corner. When it was midnight, and the giant thought that the little tailor was lying in a deep sleep, he got up, took a great iron bar, cut through the bed with one blow, and thought that he had finished off the grasshopper for good. With the earliest dawn the giants went into the forest, and had quite forgotten the little tailor, when all at once he walked up to them quite merrily and boldly. The giants were terrified, they were afraid that he would strike them all dead, and ran away in a great hurry. The little tailor went onwards, always following his own pointed nose. After he had walked for a long time, he came to the courtyard of a royal palace, and as he felt weary, he lay down on the grass and fell asleep. Whilst he lay there, the people came and inspected him on all sides, and read on his girdle: 'Seven at one stroke.' 'Ah!' said they, 'what does the great warrior here in the midst of peace? He must be a mighty lord.' They went and announced him to the King, and thought that if he should come into their service it would be of great use to him. The King then sent one of his courtiers to the little tailor to ask him if he would enter his service. The messenger stood and waited behind the sleeper until he stretched his limbs and opened his eyes, and then brought this proposal. 'For this very reason have I come here,' the tailor replied, 'I am ready to enter the King's service.' He was therefore honourably received and a special dwelling was assigned to him. The soldiers, however, were set against the little tailor, and wished him a thousand miles away. 'What is to be the end of this?' they said amongst themselves. 'If we quarrel with him, and he strikes, seven of us will fall at every blow; not one of us can stand against him.' They came therefore to a resolution, betook themselves in a body to the King, and begged for their dismissal. 'We are not prepared,' said they, 'to stay with a man who kills seven at one stroke.' The King was sorry that for the sake of one he should lose all his faithful servants, and wished that he had never set eyes on the tailor; and he would willingly have been rid of him again. But he did not dare to give him his dismissal, for he dreaded that he should strike him and all his people dead, and place himself on the throne. He thought about it for a long time, and at last hit upon a plan. He sent to the little tailor and caused him to be told that as he was such a great warrior he had one request to make to him. In a forest of his country lived two giants, who caused great mischief with their robbing, murdering, ravishing, and burning, and no one could approach them without putting himself in danger of death. If the tailor were to conquer and kill these two giants, the King would give him his only daughter to wife, and half of his kingdom as a dowry, likewise one hundred horsemen should go with him to assist him. 'That would indeed be a fine thing for a man like me!' thought the little tailor. 'One is not offered a beautiful princess and half a kingdom every day of one's life!' 'Oh, yes,' he replied, 'I will soon subdue the giants, and shall not want any of the hundred horsemen to do it; he who can hit seven with one blow need not be afraid of two.' The little tailor went into the forest, and told the hundred horsemen who were to accompany him to remain waiting outside, and he would go in first alone. He went in and looked about, and after a while he perceived both the giants. They were lying sleeping under a tree, and snoring so that the branches waved up and down. The tailor, not idle, gathered two pocketsful of stones, and with these climbed up the tree. When he was halfway up, he slipped down by a branch, until he sat just above the sleepers, and then let one stone after another fall on the breast of one of the giants. For a long time the giant felt nothing, but at last he awoke, pushed his comrade, and said: 'Why art thou knocking me?' 'Thou must be dreaming,' said the other, 'I am not knocking thee.' Then they laid themselves down to sleep again, and the tailor threw a stone down on the second. 'What is the meaning of this?' cried the other. 'Why art thou hitting me?' 'I am not hitting thee,' answered the first, growling. They disputed about it for a while, but as they were weary they let the matter rest, and their eyes closed once more. The little tailor began his game again, picked out the biggest stone, and threw it with all his might on the breast of the first giant. 'That is too bad!' cried he, and sprang up like a madman, and pushed his companion against the tree until it shook. The other paid him back in the same coin, and they got into such a rage that they tore up trees and belaboured each other so long, that at last they both fell down dead at the same time. Then the little tailor leapt down. 'It is a lucky thing,' said he, 'that they did not tear up the tree on which I was sitting, or I should have had to spring on to another like a squirrel; but tailors are nimble.' He drew out his sword and gave each of them a couple of thrusts in the breast, and then went out to the horsemen and said: 'The work is done; I have finished both of them off, but it was hard work. They tore up trees in their sore need, and defended themselves with them, but all that is to no purpose against a man like me, who strikes seven at one blow.' 'Were you not wounded?' asked the horsemen. 'You need not think of that,' answered the tailor, 'they have not bent one hair of mine.' The horsemen would not believe him, and rode into the forest; there they found the giants swimming in their blood, and round about lay the torn-up trees. The little tailor demanded of the King the promised reward; he, however, repented of his promise, and again bethought himself how he could get rid of the hero. 'Before thou receivest my daughter and the half of my kingdom,' said he to him, 'thou must perform one more heroic deed. In the forest roams a unicorn which does great harm, and thou must catch it first.' 'I fear one unicorn still less than two giants. Seven at one blow, is my affair!' The tailor took a rope and an axe with him, went out into the forest, and again bade those who were sent with him to wait outside. He had not to wait long. The unicorn soon came, and rushed directly on the tailor, as if it would spit him on its horn without more ceremony. 'Softly, softly; it can't be done as quickly as that,' said he, and stood still and waited until the animal was quite close, and then sprang nimbly behind the tree. The unicorn ran with all its strength against the tree, and stuck its horn so fast in the trunk that it had not strength enough to draw it out again, and thus it was caught. 'Now, I have got the beast,' said the tailor, and came out from behind the tree and put the rope round its neck, and then with his axe he hewed the horn out of the tree, and when all was ready he led the beast away and took it to the King. The King still would not give him the promised reward, and made a third demand. Before the wedding the tailor was to catch him a wild boar that made great havoc in the forest, and the huntsmen were to help him. 'Willingly,' said the tailor, 'that is child's play!' He did not take the huntsmen with him into the forest, and they were pleased that he did not, for the wild boar had several times received them in such a manner that they had no inclination to lie in wait for him. When the boar perceived the tailor, it ran on him with foaming mouth and whetted tusks, and was about to throw him to the ground, but the hero fled and sprang into a chapel which was near, and up to the window at once, and in one bound out again. The boar ran in after him, but the tailor ran round outside and shut the door, and the raging beast, which was much too heavy and clumsy to leap out of the window, was caught. The tailor called the huntsmen thither that they might see the prisoner with their own eyes. The hero, however, went to the King, who was now, whether he liked it or not, obliged to keep his promise, and gave him his daughter and half of his kingdom. If he had known that it was no warlike hero, but a little tailor who was standing before him, it would have gone to his heart still more than it did. The wedding was held with great magnificence and small joy, and out of a tailor a king was made. After some time the young Queen heard her husband say in his dreams at night: 'Boy, make me the doublet, and patch the pantaloons, or else I will rap the yard-measure over thine ears!' Then she discovered in what state of life the young lord had been born, and next morning she complained of her wrongs to her father, and asked him to help her to get rid of her husband, who was nothing but a tailor. The King comforted her and said: 'Leave thy bedroom door open this night, and my servants shall stand outside, and when he is asleep shall go in, bind him, and take him on board a ship which shall carry him into the wide world.' The woman was satisfied with this; but the King's armour-bearer, who had heard all, was friendly to the young lord, and revealed the whole plot to him. 'I will put a stop to this,' said the little tailor. At night he went to bed with his wife at the usual time, and when she thought that he had fallen asleep, she got up, opened the door, and then lay down again. The little tailor, who was only pretending to be asleep, began to cry out in a clear voice: 'Boy, make me the doublet and patch me the pantaloons, or I will rap the yard-measure over thine ears. I smote seven at one blow, I killed two giants, I brought away the unicorn, and caught the wild boar, and am I to fear those who are standing outside the chamber!' When these men heard the tailor speaking thus, they were overcome by a great dread, and ran away as if the wild huntsman were behind them, and none of them would venture to go near him. So the little tailor was and remained a king to the end of his life.

title: King Thrushbeard
description: A proud princess is humbled and learns to love the mocked King Thrushbeard.
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A King had a daughter who was beautiful beyond all measure, but so proud and haughty withal that no suitor was good enough for her. She sent away one after the other, and ridiculed them as well. Once the King made a great festival, and invited thereto, from far and near, all the young men likely to marry. They were all marshalled in a row according to their rank and standing; first came the kings, then the grand-dukes, then the princes, the earls, the barons, and the gentry. Then the King's daughter was led through the ranks, but to every one she had some objection to make; one was too fat, 'The wine-cask,' she said. Another was too tall, 'Long and thin has little in.' The third was too short, 'Short and thick is never quick.' The fourth was too pale, 'As pale as death.' The fifth too red, 'A turkey-cock.' The sixth was not straight enough, 'A green log dried behind the stove.' And so she had something to say against every one, but she made herself especially merry over a good King who stood quite high up in the row, and whose chin had grown a little crooked. 'Look,' cried she, and laughed, 'he has a chin like a thrush's beak!' and from that time he got the name of Thrushbeard. But the old King, when he saw that his daughter did nothing but mock the people, and despised all the suitors who were gathered there, was very angry, and swore that she should have for her husband the very first beggar that came to his doors. A few days afterwards a fiddler came and sang beneath the windows, trying to earn a small alms. When the King heard him he said: 'Let him come up.' The fiddler entered in his dirty, ragged clothes, sang before the King and his daughter, and when he had ended he asked for a trifling gift. The King said: 'Your song has pleased me so well that I will give you my daughter to wife.' The King's daughter shuddered, but the King said: 'I have sworn to give you to the very first beggar, and I will keep my word.' All pleading was in vain. The priest was brought, and she had to let herself be wedded to the fiddler on the spot. When that was done the King said: 'Now it is not proper for you, a beggar's wife, to stay any longer in my palace, you may just go away with your husband.' The beggar-man led her out by the hand, and she was obliged to walk away on foot with him. When they came to a large forest she asked: 'To whom does that beautiful forest belong?' 'It belongs to King Thrushbeard; if you had taken him, it would all have been yours.' 'Ah, unhappy girl that I am, if I had but taken King Thrushbeard!' Next they came to a meadow. 'To whom does this beautiful green meadow belong?' 'It belongs to King Thrushbeard; if you had taken him, it would all have been yours.' 'Ah, unhappy girl that I am, if I had but taken King Thrushbeard!' Then they came to a large town. 'To whom does this fine large town belong?' 'It belongs to King Thrushbeard; if you had taken him, it would all have been yours.' 'Ah, unhappy girl that I am, if I had but taken King Thrushbeard!' 'It does not please me,' said the fiddler, 'to hear you always wishing for another husband; am I not good enough for you?' At last they came to a very little hut, and she said: 'Oh, good heavens! what a small house! To whom does this miserable, tiny hut belong?' The fiddler answered: 'That is my house and yours, where we shall live together.' She had to stoop to get in at the low door. 'Where are the servants?' said the King's daughter. 'What servants?' answered the beggar-man; 'you must yourself do what you wish to have done. Just make a fire at once, and put on water to cook my supper, I am quite tired.' The King's daughter knew nothing about lighting fires or cooking, and the beggar-man had to lend a hand himself to get anything fairly done. When they had finished their scanty meal they went to bed; but the fiddler called her up quite early in the morning to clean the house. For a few days they lived in this way as well as might be, and then came to the end of their provisions. Then the man said: 'Wife, we cannot go on any longer eating and drinking here and earning nothing. You must weave baskets.' He went out, cut some willows, and brought them home. Then she began to weave, but the tough willows wounded her delicate hands. 'I see that this won't do,' said the man; 'try spinning, perhaps you will do that better.' She sat down and tried to spin, but the hard thread soon cut her soft fingers till the blood ran down. 'You see,' said the man, 'you are fit for no sort of work; I have made a bad bargain with you. Now I will try to make a business with pots and earthenware; you must sit in the market and sell the ware.' 'Alas,' thought she, 'if any of the people from my father's kingdom come to the market and see me sitting there, selling, how they will laugh at me!' But it was of no use, she had to yield unless she chose to die of hunger. For the first time she behaved herself well, for she was fair, and the people bought her wares willingly, and paid her what she asked; many of them even gave her the money and left the pots with her as well. So they lived on what she had earned as long as it lasted, then the husband bought a great many new pots. With these she seated herself in a corner of the market-place, and set them out in front of her for sale. But a drunken hussar came by, and rode his horse against her pots so that they were all broken into a thousand bits. She began to cry, and did not know what to do for fear. 'Ah, what will become of me!' said she; 'what will my husband say to this!' She ran home and told him of the misfortune. 'Who would have thought you would have been so silly as to put an earthenware stall in the corner of the market-place, where every one knocks up against it!' said he; 'but let us leave off crying. I see you are not fit for any ordinary work, so I have been to our King's palace, and have asked whether they cannot find a place for a kitchen-maid, and they have promised me to take you; in this way you will get your food for nothing.' The King's daughter was now a kitchen-maid, and had to be at the cook's beck and call, and do the dirtiest work. In both her pockets she fastened a little jar, in which she took home what was left of what was served at table, and upon this they lived. It happened that the wedding of the King's eldest son was to be celebrated, and the poor woman went up and placed herself by the door of the hall to look on. When all the candles were lit, and people, each more beautiful than the other, entered, and all was full of pomp and splendour, she thought of her lot with a sad heart, and cursed the pride and haughtiness which had humbled her and brought her so low. The smell of the delicious dishes which were being taken in and out reached her, and the servants threw her now and then a bit of them: that she put in her jars to take home. All at once the King's son entered, clothed in velvet and silk. He saw the beautiful woman standing by the door, took her by the hand, and wanted to dance with her, but she refused and shrank with fear, for she saw that it was King Thrushbeard, who was courting her, and whom she had mocked. Her struggles were of no avail; he drew her into the hall. Then the string by which her pockets were hung broke, the pots fell down, the soup ran out, and the scraps were scattered all about. When the people saw it, there was general laughter and derision, and she was so ashamed that she would have liked to have been a thousand fathoms under the ground. She sprang to the door and wanted to run away, but a man caught her and brought her back; and when she looked at him it was King Thrushbeard again. He said to her kindly: 'Be not afraid, I and the fiddler who lived with you in the wretched hut are one. For love of you I disguised myself so; and I also was the hussar who rode his horse against your pots. This was all done to humble your proud spirit, and to punish you for the insolence with which you mocked me.' Then she wept bitterly and said: 'I have done great wrong, and am not worthy to be your wife.' But he said: 'Be comforted, the evil days are past; now we will celebrate our wedding.' Then the maids-in-waiting came and put on her the most splendid clothing, and her father and his whole court were there already to wish her happiness on her marriage with King Thrushbeard, and the joy now began in earnest. I wish you and I had been there too.
